title: DAVID'S OWN SON TOOK HIS FATHER'S CONCUBINES ON A ROOFTOP—AND ALL ISRAEL WAS MEANT TO KNOW
paragraphs: DAVID'S OWN SON TOOK HIS FATHER'S CONCUBINES ON A ROOFTOP—AND ALL ISRAEL WAS MEANT TO KNOW

The son wanted his father's throne. He chose public sexual humiliation to prove he had taken it. But behind this horrifying betrayal was an older sin, a shattered family, and a warning about what happens when the wounds we refuse to confront become the weapons that destroy us.
There are betrayals that break your heart.
And then there are betrayals so cruel that you wonder whether the person who committed them ever loved you at all.
Imagine being a father.

You have made terrible mistakes. You have sinned against God. You have hurt people you should have protected. You have repented, but the consequences of your choices have continued to haunt your family.
Then one day, your own son turns against you.
He steals the loyalty of people you once led. He forces you out of your home. He takes the throne you occupied.
And as though taking your kingdom were not enough, he does something so humiliating, so calculated, and so publicly degrading that the entire nation is meant to hear about it.
He takes the women you left behind.
He goes up onto the roof of your palace.
And there, in a tent deliberately erected for public notice, he has sexual relations with your concubines.
Your own son.
Your own house.
Your own roof.
The same rooftop from which your own disastrous sin had once begun.
This is not a fictional tragedy written to shock an audience.
This is Scripture.
And what makes it even more disturbing is that the Bible had already warned David that something terrible would happen inside his own household.
But before we go any further, understand something important.
This story is not simply about a wicked son and a broken father.

It is about the devastating consequences of sin, the abuse of power, the suffering of people caught in someone else's rebellion, and the difference between being forgiven by God and being spared every earthly consequence.
And eventually, it will bring us face-to-face with a greater Son of David.
A King who did not seize His Father's throne through humiliation.
A King who willingly endured humiliation to rescue sinners.
His name is Jesus Christ.
And to understand why that matters, we must return to the rooftop.
Second Samuel 16:20–22 records the horrifying scene:
"Then said Absalom to Ahithophel, Give counsel among you what we shall do.

And Ahithophel said unto Absalom, Go in unto thy father's concubines, which he hath left to keep the house; and all Israel shall hear that thou art abhorred of thy father: then shall the hands of all that are with thee be strong.
So they spread Absalom a tent upon the top of the house; and Absalom went in unto his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel."
— 2 Samuel 16:20–22, King James Version
Read that last sentence again.
"In the sight of all Israel."
The Hebrew text makes the public nature of this act unmistakable.
The phrase is:
לְעֵינֵי כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל
Le'einei kol-Yisra'el.
Literally, "before the eyes of all Israel."
This was not a private affair driven merely by lust.
It was a political declaration.
Absalom was announcing that he had taken his father's royal position and was prepared to break with him beyond reconciliation.

In the ancient royal world, taking possession of a king's women could carry a claim to his authority. We see related tensions elsewhere in Scripture, including the accusations involving Abner and Saul's concubine in 2 Samuel 3:7–8 and Adonijah's request concerning Abishag in 1 Kings 2:13–25.
But there is a crucial detail many readers miss.
Scripture says a tent was pitched on the rooftop and that the act occurred "in the sight of all Israel." It does not require us to imagine every intimate detail being visibly exposed to the crowd.
The point is that Absalom made the act publicly known.
He wanted the nation to understand what he had done.
He wanted his father to be disgraced.
And he wanted his followers to believe there was no turning back.
This was rebellion turned into spectacle.
A son publicly dishonoring his father to strengthen his own claim to power.
And behind that spectacle were ten women whose suffering must not be forgotten.
They were not trophies.
They were not political decorations.
They were human beings.
David had left these ten concubines to care for the palace when he fled Jerusalem (2 Samuel 15:16). Absalom then used them as instruments of his political rebellion.
The biblical text does not record their consent. Given the circumstances and the severe imbalance of power, we must not romanticize what happened or treat these women as willing participants.
Their bodies became the ground on which powerful men fought for control.
And their suffering did not end when Absalom died.

Second Samuel 20:3 tells us that when David returned, he provided for these women but did not resume marital relations with them. They lived in confinement, described as living in widowhood until their deaths.
Think about that.
Absalom pursued a throne.
David endured humiliation.
But these women carried lifelong consequences from a conflict they did not create.
Sometimes the people who suffer most from a family's sin are the ones whose names history barely remembers.
And if you have ever been wounded by someone else's selfishness, someone else's appetite, someone else's ambition, or someone else's abuse of authority, there is something you need to hear.
God did not overlook those women simply because the narrative does not tell us their names.
Their suffering is preserved in His Word.
And the fact that Scripture records an evil act does not mean Scripture approves of it.
But how did David's family reach such a horrifying moment?
To understand the rooftop of Absalom's rebellion, we must return to another rooftop.
Years earlier, David had been walking on the roof of his palace when he saw Bathsheba bathing.
Second Samuel 11 describes what followed.

David sent for her. He slept with her. She became pregnant. And when his attempts to conceal the pregnancy failed, David arranged for her husband, Uriah, to be placed in a deadly position during battle.
Uriah died.
David had taken another man's wife and arranged the death of a loyal soldier.
The king who had once confronted giants was now hiding monstrous wrongdoing behind royal authority.
But God saw everything.
Second Samuel 11:27 delivers a devastating verdict:
"But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD."
There is no royal exemption from holiness.
No spiritual reputation powerful enough to erase God's moral standards.
No title, ministry, following, wealth, or public success that can make hidden evil righteous.
David was God's anointed king.
And David had sinned grievously.
Then the prophet Nathan confronted him.
Through a story about a rich man who stole a poor man's beloved lamb, Nathan exposed the king's wrongdoing.
When David condemned the guilty man in Nathan's story, the prophet answered:
"Thou art the man."
— 2 Samuel 12:7
Four words.
And the walls of David's self-deception came crashing down.
Have you ever noticed how easily we recognize sin when someone else commits it?
We can identify another person's pride.
Another person's dishonesty.
Another person's lust.
Another person's cruelty.
But when the Holy Spirit begins exposing our own hearts, suddenly we have explanations.
We were lonely.
We were hurt.
We were under pressure.
We were misunderstood.
We did not mean for things to go that far.
And sometimes those explanations contain real pain.
But pain does not automatically make our choices righteous.
David could not blame the pressure of kingship.
He could not blame Bathsheba.
He could not blame Uriah.
He could not blame his circumstances.
When Nathan confronted him, David finally said:
"I have sinned against the LORD."
— 2 Samuel 12:13
No elaborate defense.
No attempt to negotiate innocence.
Just confession.
And Nathan answered:
"The LORD also hath put away thy sin; thou shalt not die."
Here is the astonishing mercy of God.
David was guilty.
David deserved judgment.
Yet God extended forgiveness.
But forgiveness did not mean that every consequence disappeared.
Nathan had already declared in 2 Samuel 12:11–12 that calamity would arise from David's own household and that what David had done secretly would be answered by public disgrace.
The Hebrew of 2 Samuel 12:12 sharpens the contrast:
אַתָּה עָשִׂיתָ בַסָּתֶר
Attah asita vasater.
"You did it in secret."
And then:
וְאֶעֱשֶׂה אֶת־הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה נֶגֶד כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל
Ve'e'eseh et-haddavar hazzeh neged kol-Yisra'el.
"But I will do this thing before all Israel."
Secret sin.
Public disgrace.
A palace rooftop.
And years later, another palace rooftop.
The connection is horrifying.
But we must understand it carefully.

God's prophetic announcement of judgment does not make Absalom's actions morally acceptable. God can sovereignly bring judgment through events involving sinful human choices without approving those choices.
Absalom remained responsible for his rebellion and the harm he inflicted.
And David's concubines were not guilty merely because they suffered its consequences.
That distinction matters.
Because there are people who have been told that every terrible thing done to them must somehow be punishment for their own sin.
That is not what Scripture teaches.
Jesus Himself rejected the assumption that every individual tragedy can be traced to the victim's personal wrongdoing (John 9:1–3).
Do not take the consequences of another person's evil and turn them into an accusation against the wounded.
But the story grows darker still.
Because Absalom's rebellion did not appear out of nowhere.
Before the rooftop, there was a family already torn apart.
David's son Amnon had sexually violated his half-sister Tamar.
Second Samuel 13 records her anguish and the devastating injustice she endured.
Absalom, Tamar's brother, became furious.
And David, though angry, is not recorded in that chapter as bringing Amnon to justice.
For two years, Absalom carried his anger.
Then he arranged Amnon's murder.
Afterward, Absalom fled.
Later, he returned to Jerusalem, but his relationship with David remained deeply fractured.
Eventually, Absalom began cultivating public support, presenting himself as someone who would give the people the justice they sought.
Second Samuel 15:6 says that Absalom "stole the hearts of the men of Israel."
Notice the tragedy.
A family had experienced sexual violence, grief, anger, murder, estrangement, and unresolved conflict.
And out of that brokenness grew a rebellion that threatened an entire kingdom.
We should not pretend the Bible explicitly tells us every motive in Absalom's heart.
It does not.
But it does show us how a history of grave wrongdoing and fractured relationships preceded his revolt.
And there is a warning here for every family.
Unaddressed evil does not become harmless simply because people stop talking about it.
Silence is not always peace.
Distance is not always healing.
And pretending that nothing happened does not restore what was broken.
Some families are sitting at dinner tables where everyone knows something is wrong, but nobody dares speak.
Some children have grown into adulthood carrying wounds that were never acknowledged.
Some parents want reconciliation without confession.
Some relatives demand forgiveness while refusing accountability.
Some churches want the appearance of unity without confronting the wrongdoing that shattered it.
But biblical restoration is not built on denial.
It requires truth.
It requires repentance where sin has occurred.
It requires justice and protection for those who have been harmed.
And sometimes it requires boundaries even when forgiveness is sincerely offered.
Absalom's story does not excuse revenge.
His pain did not give him permission to abuse others.
But neither should his rebellion make us overlook the earlier injustices that helped shape the tragedy.
Hurt people are still morally responsible for what they do with their hurt.
And wounded people deserve care before their pain becomes another chapter of destruction.
Then came the day David fled Jerusalem.
The king who once entered the city in triumph now walked away from it in grief.
Second Samuel 15:30 describes David ascending the Mount of Olives, weeping, with his head covered and his feet bare.
Imagine that scene.
The king is crying.
His servants are crying.
The city is behind him.
His son is coming for his throne.
And David does not know how the story will end.
Perhaps you know something about that kind of heartbreak.
Not because your child seized a kingdom.
But because someone you loved became someone you no longer recognized.
A son who will not speak to you.
A daughter who carries years of anger.
A marriage destroyed by betrayal.
A friendship poisoned by jealousy.
A family inheritance turned into a battlefield.
A person you helped who now speaks against you.
A reputation damaged by someone who once knew your most vulnerable moments.
You may have experienced the terrible loneliness of realizing that the person who knows where you are weakest has decided to strike there.
David knew that pain.
And he knew something else.
He was not innocent of everything that had brought his household into crisis.
That is part of what makes his grief so complicated.
He was a sinner who had been forgiven.
A father who had failed.
A king suffering the consequences of his own wrongdoing.
And a man genuinely wounded by his son's evil.
All those realities could exist together.
That is often how real life works.
People are rarely as simple as the labels we attach to them.
A person can be responsible for terrible choices and still suffer genuine betrayal.
A person can repent sincerely and still have relationships that remain damaged.
A person can be forgiven by God and still have difficult responsibilities to face.
And a person can be deeply wounded without being permitted to wound others in return.
The Gospel does not ask us to lie about any of these realities.
It brings them into the light.
But here is where the story takes another devastating turn.
The adviser who encouraged Absalom's public violation of David's concubines was Ahithophel.
He had once been David's counselor.
Second Samuel 16:23 says his counsel was highly regarded, as though someone had consulted the word of God.
Now his wisdom was being used to strengthen rebellion.
He advised Absalom to make the break with David unmistakable.
To turn private family betrayal into a national political statement.
And Absalom listened.
This is what happens when intelligence becomes detached from righteousness.
A person can be brilliant and morally corrupt.
Strategic and spiritually blind.
Persuasive and destructive.
Not every voice that sounds wise is leading you toward God.
Some counsel will strengthen your pride while weakening your soul.
Some people will tell you exactly what your wounded ego wants to hear.
Some will encourage you to expose, humiliate, retaliate, and destroy, then call it strength.
But James 3:17 describes wisdom from above as pure, peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere.
Ahithophel's advice was politically calculated.
But it was not holy.
And Absalom's decision showed what kind of king he was becoming.
He wanted power badly enough to turn vulnerable women into instruments of humiliation.
He wanted the throne without the character required to rule it.
And this is where the story stops being merely ancient history.
Because Absalom's temptation still lives in the human heart.
We may not be standing on palace rooftops.
But we still want to win arguments by humiliating people.
We still want to expose those who embarrassed us.
We still want to prove that we have moved on by making someone else suffer.
We still want to answer rejection with revenge.
We still want to use our pain as permission to become cruel.
And sometimes, the most frightening question is not what someone has done to us.
It is what we are becoming because of what they did.
Are we healing?
Or are we rehearsing revenge?
Are we pursuing justice?
Or are we beginning to enjoy the thought of another person's destruction?
Are we surrendering our wounds to Christ?
Or are we building an identity around them?
There is a difference between seeking accountability and seeking humiliation.
There is a difference between telling the truth and weaponizing the truth.
There is a difference between refusing to tolerate evil and allowing evil to transform your own heart.
Romans 12:19 calls believers away from personal vengeance and toward trust in God's justice.
That does not mean refusing lawful protection or accountability.
It means we do not have to become instruments of cruelty to prove that cruelty was wrong.
And now comes one of the most heartbreaking details in this entire account.
Absalom's rebellion ultimately failed.
David's forces defeated the rebels.
And Absalom died.
When David received the news, he did not celebrate the death of the son who had betrayed him.
He wept.
Second Samuel 18:33 records his cry:
"O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee, O Absalom, my son, my son!"
Those words are almost unbearable.
The son had stolen his father's throne.
Humiliated his father.
Threatened his life.
And still, David cried out in grief.
"O my son."
Not "my enemy."
Not "the traitor."
"My son."
The text does not tell us that David was an exemplary father in every respect. Far from it.
It does not erase the injustice that had unfolded under his roof.
But it does show a father whose grief survived his son's betrayal.
And there is something deeply human in that.
You can love someone and be devastated by what they have done.
You can grieve a relationship that became unsafe.
You can mourn someone who rejected you.
You can recognize wrongdoing without pretending your love never existed.
Sometimes the hardest grief is not for someone who never loved you.
It is for someone you loved who chose a path you could not follow.
David's cry is heartbreaking.
But it also points us toward a greater question.
What if there were a King who could do more than wish He had died in another person's place?
What if there were a King who actually gave His life to save His enemies?
This is where the story must lead us.
Not merely to David.
Not merely to Absalom.
But to Jesus.
The New Testament identifies Jesus Christ as the promised Son of David.
In Luke 1:32–33, the angel announces that He will receive the throne of His father David and reign over a kingdom without end.
But Jesus is not another Absalom.
Absalom sought a throne through betrayal.
Jesus, the rightful King, humbled Himself in obedience to the Father.
Absalom used other people's bodies to strengthen his political power.
Jesus gave His own body for the salvation of sinners.
Absalom made humiliation a weapon against his father.
Jesus endured humiliation from sinful men while accomplishing His Father's saving purpose.
Absalom's path led to rebellion and death.
Jesus passed through death and rose again in victory.
Philippians 2:8–9 declares:
"And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name."
Consider the contrast.
Absalom wanted to be exalted, so he brought disgrace upon others.
Jesus humbled Himself, and the Father exalted Him.
Absalom tried to secure a kingdom by demonstrating that he could take what belonged to another.
Jesus established His saving reign through perfect obedience and sacrificial love.
And there is another connection worth remembering.
David crossed the Mount of Olives in tears while fleeing betrayal.
Centuries later, Jesus also approached His suffering through the Mount of Olives, knowing that betrayal and arrest were near.
These events are not identical, and we should not force every detail into a symbolic prediction.
But the contrast is spiritually powerful.
David was a flawed king suffering in a world scarred by his own sins and the sins of others.
Jesus was the sinless King who willingly suffered for sinners.
David cried that he wished he could have died in Absalom's place.
Jesus actually died for the ungodly.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Not that God ignores sin.
Not that betrayal does not matter.
Not that victims must pretend their wounds are insignificant.
Not that repentance is optional.
But that Jesus Christ entered a world filled with guilt, injustice, rebellion, shame, and suffering, and gave Himself as the atoning sacrifice for sinners.
He was crucified.
He was buried.
He rose from the dead.
And through Him, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered to those who repent and believe.
The Greek word often translated "repentance" is μετάνοια, metanoia.
It refers to a change of mind and heart that turns a person away from sin and toward God.
Biblical repentance is more than feeling embarrassed after being exposed.
It is more than regretting that consequences arrived.
It is a genuine turning toward God, expressed in a changed direction of life.
David's confession in Psalm 51 helps us see that kind of repentance.
He prayed:
"Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me."
— Psalm 51:10
In Hebrew:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
"Create for me a clean heart, O God."
Not merely a repaired reputation.
Not a better excuse.
Not a way to escape embarrassment.
A clean heart.
David needed something deeper than image restoration.
And so do we.
Because the deepest problem in our lives is not always what other people know about us.
Sometimes it is what God knows about us that we keep refusing to face.
The envy.
The bitterness.
The secret dishonesty.
The unforgiveness we are nurturing.
The sexual sin we keep justifying.
The pride that makes confession feel unbearable.
The anger we have begun to enjoy.
The way we have used people to satisfy our desires.
The way we have avoided responsibility because admitting the truth would cost us something.
Jesus did not come simply to make our public image more respectable.
He came to save sinners and transform hearts.
And perhaps that is why this story feels so uncomfortable.
Because somewhere in it, we recognize ourselves.
Sometimes we are like David, desperately needing to stop hiding and confess.
Sometimes we are tempted to become like Absalom, allowing wounded pride to turn into destructive choices.
Sometimes we are like those ten women, suffering because someone with power treated us as though our dignity did not matter.
And sometimes we are simply standing among the broken pieces of a family, wondering whether anything good can ever grow there again.
But hear this carefully.
You are not required to pretend that evil was good in order to receive God's healing.
You do not have to excuse an abuser to honor Christ.
You do not have to return to an unsafe relationship to prove that you have forgiven.
And you do not have to deny your own wrongdoing in order to believe that grace is possible.
The cross tells the truth about both sin and mercy.
Sin is so serious that the Son of God gave His life to save us.
Grace is so extraordinary that even guilty sinners may come to Him for forgiveness.
First John 1:9 declares that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
But that promise is not permission to continue harming others.
True repentance bears fruit.
Where restitution is possible, we should pursue it.
Where accountability is required, we should accept it.
Where someone has been harmed, their safety and dignity must matter.
And where reconciliation is not presently possible, we can still seek to walk faithfully before God.
This is what makes grace so different from denial.
Grace does not call darkness light.
Grace brings sinners into the light so they can be changed.
And if you have reached this point with tears in your eyes, anger in your chest, or a memory you have never fully spoken about, perhaps this is the moment to be honest with God.
Not with a performance.
Not with polished religious language.
Just honesty.
"Lord, I am hurt."
"Lord, I have sinned."
"Lord, I am angry."
"Lord, I have been hiding."
"Lord, I do not know how to forgive."
"Lord, I need help."
He already knows.
And He invites you to come.
You do not owe the internet the details of your pain. You do not have to reveal a traumatic experience publicly to prove your sincerity.
But if you want prayer, let this be a place where brothers and sisters in Christ can respond with compassion rather than condemnation.

And if you have a testimony of how Jesus has led you from shame toward repentance, from bitterness toward forgiveness, or from spiritual exhaustion toward renewed faith, your words may encourage someone who has almost given up.
Someone reading may be one prayer away from asking for help.
One honest confession away from beginning the process of restoration.
One act of courage away from refusing to repeat the sins that wounded their family.
That is why stories like this matter.
Not because scandal is entertaining.
But because Scripture refuses to hide the reality of human brokenness.
And because Jesus Christ is greater than the darkness that brokenness reveals.
This is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior.
Not because the past becomes imaginary.
Not because consequences vanish.
Not because every broken relationship is automatically restored in this lifetime.
But because the risen Christ offers forgiveness, new life, and a future that does not have to be ruled by the sins of yesterday.
And if this message has strengthened your faith, please do not let it end with you.
Send it privately to a person who needs encouragement.
There is also a deeper way to stand with this ministry.
Gospel Warrior is working to make biblical teaching, Christian literature, and discipleship resources accessible to more people.

The mission is to keep nourishing believers, helping people understand Scripture, and reaching those who may never enter a church building but are willing to read a message about Jesus on their phone.
That work requires time, resources, and faithful support.
Scripture encourages generous, willing giving.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
That means no one should be pressured into giving.
You do not have to pay for God's favor.
And your standing before God is never measured by a monthly payment.
Salvation is the gift of grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not something purchased through financial support.
But if you believe in the work Gospel Warrior is doing, your monthly contribution can be a meaningful way to help sustain and expand it.
These items are not the reason to give.
They are simply a small expression of gratitude for those who choose to stand alongside the ministry.
You can still be part of this mission.
Read the Word.
Pray for the ministry.
Encourage someone who is struggling.
Speak the truth in love.
Your prayers, your witness, and your willingness to point another person toward Jesus matter deeply.
Because the goal has never been merely to grow a page.
It is to make Christ known.
To call sinners to repentance.
To remind wounded people that their suffering is seen.
To help believers grow in the truth.
And to proclaim that no human scandal is beyond the reach of the Gospel's invitation to repentance and grace.
Now return with me, one final time, to that rooftop in Jerusalem.
A son wanted to prove that he had conquered his father.
He used humiliation to announce his power.
He believed that taking what belonged to another man would make him king.
But his kingdom did not last.
His rebellion ended.
His life ended.
And his father was left weeping.
Then look toward another hill, centuries later.
There stands Jesus Christ.
Mocked.
Rejected.
Stripped of His garments.
Crowned with thorns.
Crucified beneath a public accusation.
He did not climb a throne by disgracing the helpless.
He went to the cross to redeem the guilty.
He did not need to steal a kingdom.
He was the rightful King.
And when He rose from the dead, He demonstrated a victory no earthly rebellion could ever achieve.
Victory over sin and death.
So perhaps the most important question is not what Absalom did on the rooftop.
Perhaps the most important question is what you will do with the Savior who went to the cross.
Will you continue hiding?
Will you keep defending what God is calling you to confess?
Will you let the people who hurt you determine the kind of person you become?
Or will you bring your guilt, your grief, your anger, and your brokenness to Jesus Christ?
You cannot change what happened yesterday.
But by God's grace, you can turn toward Christ today.
Repent where you have sinned.
Seek help where you have been harmed.
Choose truth over appearances.
Choose obedience over revenge.
And trust the Savior whose mercy is greater than the shame you thought would define you forever.
Because the rooftop revealed how far human rebellion can fall.
But the cross revealed how far divine love was willing to go to save sinners.
The scandal may be part of your history, but through Jesus Christ, it does not have to be the final word over your eternity.
